hypothesis.title: The Scale That Holds
hypothesis.question: When a short loop is transformed, which representation scale best predicts whether listeners still hear it as the same musical object: low-frequency modulation, critical-band separation, phase/pitch coherence, or harmonic graph adjacency?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a loop's identity is carried primarily by one representation scale, then damaging that scale while preserving the others will reduce perceived coherence and recognizability more than damaging a non-primary scale.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: The selected sources converge on a resolution-contract problem: each useful representation preserves a different layer of musical information. Rhythm-formant analysis treats speech rhythm as low-frequency amplitude modulation and separates macro-temporal structure from finer spectral features [S1]. Tonnetz theory formalizes harmonic continuity as graph/geometric adjacency rather than waveform similarity [S2]. WST-X warns that too much temporal averaging can erase fine spectral artifacts, so stability must be balanced against sensitivity [S3]. Speech-recognition fairness results show that encoder design and compression can dominate downstream behavior, including hallucination under silence or masking [S4]. Bark-scale dynamics frames frequency processing around perceptual critical bands rather than arbitrary crossovers [S5]. PHALAR suggests pitch- and phase-equivariant representations preserve musical coherence better than phase-discarding semantic baselines [S6]. Together, these imply a testable compositional claim: the layer that carries identity in a given loop can be located by selectively damaging candidate representation scales while holding the others constant.

recipe.title: Resolution Switching Loop Test
recipe.bodyMd: Create one eight-bar loop whose identity could plausibly live at several scales: a tremolo or sidechained pad supplies a clear low-frequency modulation profile [S1], a two-voice midrange texture can either share or avoid Bark-like critical-band regions [S5], a kick/bass or doubled-synth pair exposes phase alignment [S6], and a four-chord progression moves by close harmonic adjacency [S2]. Render a control version, then four test versions that each damage only one scale. Version A smears the modulation profile while preserving notes, harmony, phase, and spectrum. Version B crowds the midrange voices into the same perceptual band while preserving rhythm and harmony. Version C offsets or rotates phase alignment while preserving spectral balance. Version D replaces graph-adjacent chord motion with arbitrary chord changes while preserving sound design and modulation. Disconfirming evidence: if listeners cannot reliably distinguish the targeted damage conditions from the control, or if all damage types reduce identity equally, then the loop does not have a dominant representation scale under this protocol. Keep degradation moderate; S3 and S4 both warn that excessive averaging or degradation can collapse distinctions globally rather than reveal the meaningful layer.

parameters.value: Target modulation-center frequency: 2 Hz control, smeared to competing 1 Hz and 4 Hz pulses in Version A
Critical-band condition: separate vs crowded midrange energy neighborhoods
Phase condition: aligned control vs 90-degree and 180-degree offsets in low-frequency layer
Harmonic condition: close graph-adjacent chord motion vs arbitrary replacement progression

dawChecklist: Create an eight-bar loop at 120 BPM with drums, bass, pad/tremolo layer, two midrange voices, and four chords.
Render the control and write down the intended identity carrier before making variants.
Version A: keep MIDI/harmony fixed, but alter tremolo, sidechain, or gain automation so the dominant energy pulse no longer centers around the control rate.
Version B: keep notes/timing fixed, but EQ or transpose two midrange layers so they mask each other in the same perceptual frequency neighborhood.
Version C: keep levels/EQ fixed, but offset the phase of the bass/doubled layer by 90 degrees and 180 degrees; choose the strongest identity-changing render.
Version D: keep rhythm, timbre, phase, and mix fixed, but replace the chord path with non-adjacent/arbitrary moves.
Level-match all renders within 0.5 dB LUFS so loudness is not the cue.
Blind-rank the five renders for recognizability, coherence, and 'same loop' identity; note which damaged scale causes the largest drop.

protocol.listeningContext: Level-matched blind A/B/X-style listening on headphones and monitors.
protocol.listeningMethod: Rate each render 1-5 for recognizability, coherence, and identity preservation; repeat after a ten-minute break.
whatStaysConstant: melodic contour outside the targeted harmonic condition

notes: Companion essay written to docs/essays/the-scale-that-holds.md. This run frames the connection as a representation-scale problem rather than a generic fidelity problem.
